title: What Do Verifiable Rewards Teach Video–Language Models About Time? A Controlled Multi-Model Study

paper.title:
What Do Verifiable Rewards Teach Video–Language Models About Time?
A Controlled Multi-Model Study
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has produced large
reasoning gains in language models, and verifiable video benchmarks make the
recipe directly applicable to causal–temporal video question answering. We
present a controlled study of what RLVR actually teaches video–language
models about temporal structure. We fine-tune four open models
(Qwen3-VL-8B/4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) with group relative policy
optimization (GRPO) under three data
recipes: verified (synthetic CLEVRER-derived questions with exact
answer and event-order rewards), unverified (self-supervised pretext
tasks over 43,751 real web videos), and a 1:1 mixture , plus a
targeted verified+real arm that augments the verified data with
4,000 verifiable questions on real video. A
pre-registered protocol evaluates every model–recipe cell on a held-out
in-domain test set and on out-of-domain real video: a temporal stress set
built from NExT-QA and a broad-coverage subset of the MVBench temporal
benchmark, each under three input conditions: frames in true order, frames
shuffled, and no frames. We report four findings. (1) Verified-reward
training yields large in-domain gains that shrink as base competence grows
(+14 to +19 points on weaker models; +6 on the strongest base model).
(2) A
substantial fraction of the gain is non-visual: accuracy with no
frames rises nearly as much as accuracy with frames, indicating the policy
learns answer priors and format in addition to perception. (3) Verified-only
training can severely degrade out-of-domain competence without any
indication during training: Qwen3-VL-8B loses 26.7 and 25.2 points
on the two independent real-video test sets, with losses distributed
across every question category, whereas the mixed recipe never
significantly degrades any model trained on it, on either set. The
verified+real arm removes the degradation ( − 2.3 -2.3 points, within noise
of base) while retaining a + 9.3 +9.3 -point in-domain gain, isolating narrow
synthetic-only data, rather than verification itself, as the cause. (4) No
recipe induces temporal-order grounding, operationalized as the paired
ordered-versus-shuffled accuracy difference: across 41 evaluations this
diagnostic is statistically
indistinguishable from zero in 39 and marginal in the remaining two, even
though training explicitly rewarded event
ordering and the stress set targets order-dependent questions. We conclude
that verifiable rewards improve benchmark accuracy without conferring
temporal understanding, that no-frame controls should accompany reported
gains, and that diversifying the training distribution with real video –
whether verified or unverified – provides an effective
safeguard against out-of-domain degradation.
We release the full training, evaluation, and analysis pipeline.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Film editors have long exploited the fact that the meaning of a sequence of images depends on their order: the Kuleshov effect and the montage tradition demonstrate that viewers construct causal and narrative interpretations from juxtaposition rather than from shots in isolation [ 9 , 5 , 2 ] . For video–language models this classical observation yields a concrete, falsifiable test: a model that genuinely uses temporal structure should lose accuracy when the frames it conditions on are shuffled, whereas a model that answers from per-frame content alone should not. Prior work, including our own, has found that frame-order sensitivity in current models is weak or absent even on causal benchmarks [ 14 ] . A natural hypothesis is that this deficiency is a training problem. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards has recently produced significant reasoning improvements in language models [ 17 , 4 , 12 ] : when the correctness of an output can be checked programmatically, policy optimization can climb the reward without human preference labels. Causal–temporal video QA appears ideally suited to this recipe. Synthetic benchmarks such as CLEVRER [ 19 ] provide exact answers, ground-truth event orders, and unlimited generation, so a reward can score not only the final answer but the temporal claims a model makes along the way. If any training signal can teach a model to use frame order, a reward that credits correctly ordered events should. This paper asks, with a controlled experimental design, what RLVR training actually changes in a video–language model. Three properties are distinguishable and, we show, empirically separable: (i) in-domain answer accuracy; (ii) transfer of that accuracy to out-of-domain, real-video questions; and (iii) temporal grounding, operationalized as the paired ordered-versus-shuffled accuracy difference on held-out items. Our design crosses four open model families with three data recipes – verified synthetic data with exact rewards, unverified real video with self-supervised pretext rewards, and a 1:1 mixture – plus a targeted fourth arm that augments the verified data with real-video verifiable questions, and evaluates every cell under a pre-registered protocol with clustered bootstrap confidence intervals, disjoint train/test scene splits, and cryptographic test-set fingerprints to guarantee identical items across comparisons. The results separate the three properties cleanly. Verified-reward GRPO reliably improves in-domain accuracy, with gains inversely related to the base model’s initial competence. However, a blind control, in which the model is evaluated with no frames at all, reveals that a large share of the gain is non-visual: policies acquire benchmark priors and answer formatting alongside any perceptual improvement. Out of domain, the verified-only recipe proves hazardous: Qwen3-VL-8B lost 26.7 and 25.2 points on two independent real-video test sets after verified-only training, whereas models trained on the mixture never significantly degraded, and augmenting the verified data with real verified questions restored base-level transfer – isolating data narrowness, not verification, as the cause. Finally, on the property the reward most directly targeted, we observe no effect: across 41 model–recipe–test evaluations, shuffling the input frames produced no reliable loss of accuracy in any condition, including on a stress set of questions selected to require temporal order. To our knowledge, this is the first multi-model, multi-recipe controlled study of verifiable-reward reinforcement learning for video reasoning. It establishes that the accuracy gains such training produces should not be interpreted as temporal understanding, that no-frame controls are necessary to audit what was learned, and that incorporating inexpensive unverified video into the training distribution constitutes an effective safeguard against out-of-domain degradation at negligible additional cost. The ordered/shuffled/blind evaluation protocol, the reward suite with its anti-gaming guards, and the full pipeline are released for reuse.

sections.heading: Temporal order and montage.
sections.text: That ordered juxtaposition creates meaning absent from individual images is foundational in film theory: Kuleshov’s editing experiments [ 9 ] and Eisenstein’s montage writings [ 5 ] document that interpretation is constructed between shots, a view elaborated by modern film scholarship [ 2 ] . We adopt this observation as motivation for a diagnostic – if meaning derives from order, then destroying order should impair a system that genuinely exploits it – rather than as a novel claim. In machine learning, shuffling and single-frame controls have shown that video–language benchmarks are often solvable without temporal information [ 3 , 13 ] ; those studies characterize benchmarks and pretrained models , whereas we ask whether targeted reinforcement learning can change the property, extending the control to paired per-item statistics with clustered uncertainty estimates measured before and after training.

sections.heading: Causal–temporal video benchmarks.
sections.text: CLEVRER [ 19 ] isolates collision causality with descriptive, explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual questions over synthetic physics scenes and provides exact ground truth, making it a natural source of verifiable rewards. NExT-QA [ 18 ] targets temporal and causal questions on real web video. MVBench [ 10 ] assembles twenty temporal subtasks from ground-truth annotations of six video sources, VCRBench [ 16 ] evaluates long-form causal chains via clip reordering, and ChainReaction [ 15 ] structures causal-why QA around explicit causal chains. We train on CLEVRER-derived items (verified arm) and evaluate out-of-domain transfer on NExT-QA-derived temporal items and a broad MVBench subset, keeping all test sets video-disjoint from all training data.

sections.heading: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.
sections.text: Group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [ 17 ] optimizes a policy against group-normalized rewards without a value network and underlies recent reasoning-focused post-training [ 4 ] . RLVR [ 12 ] formalizes training against programmatically checkable answers. Applications to multimodal models have focused on answer-level rewards for image reasoning; systematic evidence about what such training changes in video models – beyond benchmark scores – is scarce. Our study fills this gap with controls (shuffled and blind inputs, out-of-domain sets) designed to decompose the learned change.

sections.heading: Self-supervised video pretext tasks.
sections.text: Temporal pretext tasks – ordering shuffled clips, verifying arrow of time, anticipating future frames – have a long history in video representation learning. Our unverified arm ports these ideas to policy optimization: rewards are computed from the video itself (e.g., reconstructing the true position of frames), so tens of thousands of unlabeled web videos [ 6 ] become training signal with no annotation cost.

sections.heading: 3.1 Policy optimization
sections.text: Let π θ \pi_{\theta} be a vision–language model that maps a prompt x x (interleaved instruction text and K K video frames) to a text completion y y . For each training prompt we sample a group of G G completions y 1 , … , y G ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y_{1},\dots,y_{G}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) , score each with a scalar reward R ⁡ ( y g , x ) R(y_{g},x) (Sec. 3.2 ), and apply GRPO [ 17 ] : the advantage of y g y_{g} is its reward standardized within the group, A g = R ⁡ ( y g , x ) − mean g ′ ⁡ R ⁡ ( y g ′ , x ) std g ′ ⁡ R ⁡ ( y g ′ , x ) , A_{g}\;=\;\frac{R(y_{g},x)-\operatorname{mean}_{g^{\prime}}R(y_{g^{\prime}},x)}{\operatorname{std}_{g^{\prime}}R(y_{g^{\prime}},x)}, (1) and the policy gradient is taken on token log-probabilities weighted by A g A_{g} . We use G = 8 G{=}8 completions per prompt, LoRA adapters [ 8 ] (rank 32, α = 64 \alpha{=}64 , dropout 0.05, attention projections) on a frozen bf16 base model, learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , effective batch size 8 prompts per step, and 1,200 optimizer steps per run. Sampling uses a colocated vLLM engine [ 11 ] with per-token truncated importance-sampling correction between the sampler and trainer log-probabilities. 1 1 1 The library default, which masks whole sequences on the exponentiated sum of per-token discrepancies, silently zeroes essentially all gradients at realistic vision–language numerics; the supplementary material documents this and other failure modes we corrected, each of which produced healthy-looking but non-learning runs. Each prompt carries K = 8 K{=}8 frames sampled uniformly from the clip, capped at 401,408 401{,}408 pixels per frame. After training, adapters are merged into the base weights and all evaluation is performed on the merged model by the same serving stack used for base models, so trained and untrained checkpoints are measured identically.

sections.heading: 3.2 Verifiable rewards
sections.text: The reward is a weighted sum R = r ans + r ord + 0.2 ​ r fmt R=r_{\text{ans}}+r_{\text{ord}}+0.2\,r_{\text{fmt}} of three programmatically checkable terms. Definition 1 (Answer reward) For multiple-choice items with gold letter a ⋆ a^{\star} and choice set C C , r ans ( y ) = 𝟏 [ parse ( y ) = a ⋆ ] r_{\text{ans}}(y)=\mathbf{1}[\operatorname{parse}(y)=a^{\star}] , where parse \operatorname{parse} extracts the letter from a delimited answer block and accepts only members of C C . Definition 2 (Order reward) For items with a ground-truth event or clip order σ ⋆ \sigma^{\star} over n n elements, the completion’s stated order σ ^ \hat{\sigma} is parsed from the answer block; r ord ​ ( y ) = ( τ ⁡ ( σ ^ , σ ⋆ ) + 1 ) / 2 r_{\text{ord}}(y)=(\tau(\hat{\sigma},\sigma^{\star})+1)/2 , where τ \tau is the Kendall rank correlation, and r ord = 0 r_{\text{ord}}{=}0 if no order is parseable. r fmt r_{\text{fmt}} pays small credit for a structured response (a scene summary, a causal chain that cites specific frames, and a delimited answer). Two guards prevent reward gaming, both added after observed exploits: blocks that parrot the instruction text earn nothing, and order parsing is restricted to the delimited answer block so that frame citations inside chain-of-thought text cannot be harvested as an ordering the model never asserted. Reward terms that are constant within a completion group cancel exactly in Eq. 1 ; we verified each term has within-group variance on real batches.

sections.heading: Verified (V).
sections.text: Multiple-choice and event-ordering items derived from CLEVRER [ 19 ] train scenes, where r ans r_{\text{ans}} and r ord r_{\text{ord}} are exact. Train, validation, and test splits are scene-disjoint.

sections.heading: Unverified (U).
sections.text: Self-supervised pretext items over FineVideo [ 6 ] , a corpus of 43,751 43{,}751 real web videos (3,425 hours) we ingest and segment. Tasks include temporal jigsaw (recover the true position of shuffled frames) and anticipation (select which candidate frame follows a prefix). Both are scored by the reward terms of Sec. 3.2 – r ord r_{\text{ord}} over the stated frame order for jigsaw, r ans r_{\text{ans}} over the candidate choice for anticipation – with ground truth computed from the video itself, so no annotation is used and no reward term is unique to either arm. Held-out videos are excluded at the corpus level.

sections.heading: Mixed (V+U).
sections.text: A 1:1 interleaving of the two sources at the prompt level, holding total optimization steps fixed, so the comparison against V isolates the effect of diversifying the reward distribution rather than training longer.

sections.heading: Verified+Real (V+R).
sections.text: A targeted arm, run on Qwen3-VL-8B, that keeps every reward term and hyperparameter of V but augments the CLEVRER items with 4,000 4{,}000 multiple-choice questions from the NExT-QA train split (causal and temporal types), whose exact answers make them verifiable. Because V and V+R differ only in training data, the comparison separates two candidate causes of any out-of-domain effect of V: verified-reward optimization itself versus the narrowness of a single synthetic source. As this arm trains on NExT-QA, the temporal stress set (built from the video-disjoint validation split, Sec. 4 ) is near-domain rather than out-of-domain for it; the MVBench set remains fully out of domain for every arm.

sections.heading: 3.4 Models
sections.text: We train Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 1 ] , and Gemma-3-12B [ 7 ] – two vendors, two architecture generations, and a 3 × \times scale range. All four receive the V recipe; the three Qwen models receive all three recipes, and Qwen3-VL-8B additionally receives the V+R arm (the Gemma U/V+U cells did not complete within our compute budget and are omitted rather than partially reported). Two further candidates were excluded for cause, documented in the supplementary material: Gemma-3-4B scores below the random floor on the task (0.3% ordered accuracy), which makes every GRPO group’s rewards identical and the gradient identically zero; and InternVL3.5-14B / VideoLLaMA3-7B could not be served faithfully by the sampling stack (dynamic-tiling and unsupported-architecture incompatibilities, respectively).

sections.heading: Test sets.
sections.text: The in-domain set contains n = 300 n{=}300 multiple-choice items from CLEVRER validation scenes, scene-disjoint from all training data. Two out-of-domain sets probe transfer to real video. The temporal stress set contains n = 300 n{=}300 multiple-choice items built from NExT-QA [ 18 ] temporal questions. The broad set contains n = 306 n{=}306 items sampled evenly from nine MVBench [ 10 ] subtasks spanning six source datasets (SSv2, Moments-in-Time, FunQA, Perception Test, MoVQA scenes, and VLN); we exclude MVBench’s five CLEVRER-derived subtasks, whose videos share our verified training domain, along with license-gated, frame-folder-format, and segment-bounded subtasks (scoping rationale in the supplementary material). Every evaluation embeds a SHA-256 fingerprint of its item identifiers in its output; all evaluations of a given test set share one fingerprint, so every reported comparison is over identical items.

sections.heading: Input conditions.
sections.text: Each item is evaluated under three conditions: ordered (frames in true temporal order), shuffled (the same frames, deterministically permuted per item), and blind (no frames). Ordered accuracy measures task performance; the paired ordered − - shuffled difference measures temporal grounding; blind accuracy measures how much of the task is solvable from the question text and learned priors alone. Definition 3 (Order sensitivity) For items i = 1 , … , n i=1,\dots,n with per-item correctness c i ord , c i shuf ∈ { 0 , 1 } c^{\mathrm{ord}}_{i},c^{\mathrm{shuf}}_{i}\in\{0,1\} , order sensitivity is Δ ord = 1 n ​ ∑ i ( c i ord − c i shuf ) \Delta_{\mathrm{ord}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i}(c^{\mathrm{ord}}_{i}-c^{\mathrm{shuf}}_{i}) , with uncertainty from a bootstrap that resamples videos (clusters), not items.

sections.heading: Statistics.
sections.text: All intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap CIs with cluster resampling at the video level, which is conservative when multiple items share a source video. Decoding is greedy (temperature 0 0 ) for all evaluations. The harness refuses items without a well-formed multiple-choice prompt and reports error, empty-response, and structured-format rates alongside accuracy; no reported evaluation produced an errored or empty generation, so differences are not artifacts of failed generations. We report uncertainty intervals throughout rather than binary significance tests; with 41 evaluation cells, readers should interpret individual marginal intervals with the usual multiplicity caution – our conclusions rest on the direction and consistency of effects across models, not on any single cell.

sections.heading: Reproducibility.
sections.text: Every number in this paper is generated by script from archived evaluation artifacts; no result is transcribed by hand. Data builds, splits, and frame shuffling are deterministic (fixed seeds), training uses a pinned configuration per arm with a run-signature guard that refuses to resume a checkpoint under changed semantics, and evaluations embed the test-set fingerprint they were scored on. The full training, evaluation, and analysis pipeline – including the failure-mode guards documented in the supplementary material – will be released.

sections.heading:
5.1 Verified rewards improve in-domain accuracy inversely to base
competence
sections.text: Every model improves in-domain under the V recipe: + 14.3 +14.3 points on Qwen3-VL-8B ( 0.467 → 0.610 0.467\to 0.610 ), + 17.3 +17.3 on Qwen3-VL-4B, + 19.3 +19.3 on Gemma-3-12B, and + 6.3 +6.3 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. The ordering is informative: Qwen2.5-VL-7B begins with the highest accuracy ( 0.607 0.607 ) and gains the least, with all three of its recipes statistically indistinguishable from one another, whereas the two weakest initial models (Gemma-3-12B at 0.083 0.083 , Qwen3-VL-4B at 0.147 0.147 ) gain the most. Verifiable-reward reinforcement learning is thus most effective precisely where the base model has not already internalized the task, and its returns diminish sharply with base competence. The recipes differentiate by model. On Qwen3-VL-8B the unverified recipe reduces in-domain accuracy ( − 7.7 -7.7 ), as pretext tasks alone draw the policy away from the benchmark distribution, whereas on Qwen3-VL-4B the same recipe is the most effective single source ( + 22.0 +22.0 ). The mixture is never the worst recipe and is the best on Qwen3-VL-4B ( + 25.7 +25.7 ).

sections.heading: 5.2 A blind control reveals non-visual gains
sections.text: Accuracy with no frames rises under training in nearly every cell: 0.263 → 0.420 0.263\to 0.420 on Qwen3-VL-8B (V), 0.147 → 0.383 0.147\to 0.383 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B (V+U). Because the blind condition contains no visual information, this gain is attributable entirely to prior and format learning: the policy learns which answers are likely and how to express them. The effect transfers out of domain: on the MVBench subset, the blind accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B rises from 0.150 0.150 at base to 0.395 0.395 – 0.431 0.431 under every recipe (Table 3 ); much of what RLVR training imparts survives domain shift precisely because it never depended on the visual input. The visually attributable gain, ordered accuracy minus blind accuracy, changes far less: for Qwen3-VL-8B it is 0.203 0.203 at base and 0.190 0.190 after verified training. A benchmark improvement of 14 points therefore decomposes into predominantly non-visual learning that a standard evaluation would have attributed to perception. We contend that no-frame controls should be standard practice when reporting reinforcement learning gains on multimodal benchmarks.

sections.heading:
5.3 Verified-only training degrades out-of-domain competence;
mixing is protective
sections.text: Figure 2 : The verified-only collapse replicates on two independent out-of-domain test sets, and diversifying the verified data removes it (colors as in Fig. 1 ). Verified-only training costs Qwen3-VL-8B 26.7 points on the NExT-QA temporal stress set and 25.2 points on the MVBench broad subset; the verified+real arm (light blue), which differs from verified only in its training data, remains at base level on both sets, and the mixed recipe remains statistically indistinguishable from base or improves upon it in every cell. Error bars are 95% clustered-bootstrap CIs. On the real-video stress set (Table 2 , Fig. 2 a), verified-only training severely degraded Qwen3-VL-8B: the model falls from 0.707 0.707 to 0.440 0.440 ordered accuracy, a 26.7 26.7 -point regression on a domain its training never touched, with losses distributed broadly across items (95 items lost against 15 gained) and across all three temporal question categories (per-category breakdown in the supplementary material). The degradation replicates on the MVBench broad subset (Table 3 , Fig. 2 b): the same checkpoint falls from 0.621 0.621 to 0.369 0.369 ( − 25.2 -25.2 ), declining on every one of the nine subtasks, most severely on character ordering ( 0.853 → 0.118 0.853\to 0.118 ), despite training that directly rewarded event ordering. The same recipe does not degrade models with weaker base performance: Qwen3-VL-4B gains out of domain on both sets ( + 2.7 +2.7 stress, + 8.2 +8.2 broad) and Gemma-3-12B gains + 22.2 +22.2 on the broad set. The failure is therefore model-dependent, and, critically, it is undetectable from the training signal: neither the reward curves nor in-domain validation distinguishes the two outcomes. The mixed recipe never significantly degraded any model on either out-of-domain set (largest decline − 3.9 -3.9 points, with confidence intervals overlapping base; up to + 11.4 +11.4 on Qwen3-VL-4B) while retaining roughly two-thirds of the verified in-domain gain on the 8B model and all of it on the 4B model. Unverified real-video data thus serves a regularizing role: its rewards cannot be satisfied through benchmark-specific priors, and it anchors the policy to the distribution on which deployment occurs.

sections.heading: Isolating the cause.
sections.text: The collapse admits two explanations: verified-reward optimization itself narrows the policy, or the verified data is too narrow (a single synthetic source). The V+R arm separates them, because it changes only the data: same rewards, same hyperparameters, with 4,000 4{,}000 real-video verifiable questions added to the CLEVRER items. On MVBench, which remains fully out of domain for this arm, the degradation disappears: 0.598 0.598 against a base of 0.621 0.621 ( − 2.3 -2.3 points, confidence intervals overlapping), where V lost 25.2 25.2 . The arm simultaneously retains a + 9.3 +9.3 -point in-domain gain ( 0.467 → 0.560 0.467\to 0.560 , Table 1 ), about two-thirds of V’s, and matches base on the (for this arm, near-domain) stress set ( 0.697 0.697 vs. 0.707 0.707 ). The out-of-domain collapse is therefore a property of narrow synthetic-only verified data rather than of verifiable rewards as such, and it has two effective remedies at equal compute: diversify the verified data with real-video questions (V+R), or mix in unverified real video (V+U).

sections.heading: 5.4 No recipe induces temporal-order grounding
sections.text: Figure 3 : Order sensitivity is null essentially everywhere. Paired ordered − - shuffled accuracy differences with 95% clustered-bootstrap CIs; each row is one model–recipe, with one marker per test set (41 cells in total). Thirty-nine intervals cross zero, and the two exceptions are marginal (lower bounds ≤ 0.01 \leq 0.01 ) and inconsistent across recipes and test sets. Across all 41 evaluations (Fig. 3 ) – four models, up to four recipes, three test sets – the order-sensitivity estimate Δ ord \Delta_{\mathrm{ord}} is statistically indistinguishable from zero in 39 cells, with point estimates as often negative as positive; the two interval exceptions (Qwen3-VL-4B base and unverified on the broad set, lower bounds 0.010 0.010 and 0.003 0.003 ) are marginal, do not persist across recipes or test sets, and are consistent with what multiplicity predicts at this cell count. The null holds (i) on the stress set constructed specifically from temporal questions, (ii) after training in which event ordering was directly and substantially rewarded ( r ord r_{\text{ord}} at full weight), and (iii) for every recipe, including the one that improved in-domain accuracy by 25.7 points and the V+R arm trained directly on real-video temporal questions. Models improve on temporal benchmarks while remaining indifferent to temporal order : they answer from per-frame content, question priors, and, on synthetic data, learned answer statistics. We conclude that answer- and order-level verifiable rewards, at this scale and with this optimizer, do not induce temporal grounding; optimization instead exploits capabilities that are more readily improved, and these suffice to saturate the reward.

sections.heading: Why rewards fail to reach temporal structure.
sections.text: Policy optimization preferentially exploits whichever sources of reward are most readily improved. Our decomposition identifies at least three such sources that require less capability change than order grounding: answer-format compliance (immediate reward from r fmt r_{\text{fmt}} and parseability), question/answer priors (visible in the blind gains), and per-frame recognition (sufficient for most benchmark items, as the shuffled condition demonstrates). A reward that assigns credit only when order is decision-relevant – for instance, items constructed so that the shuffled answer differs from the ordered answer – is a natural next step; our results establish that merely rewarding correct orderings of recognizable events is insufficient, because the events can be ordered from appearance cues without temporal integration.

sections.heading: Practical guidance.
sections.text: For practitioners applying RLVR to video models, our results support three recommendations: report no-frame controls alongside headline gains; evaluate at least one out-of-domain set before and after training, with identical items enforced by fingerprinting; and diversify the training distribution of any verified-reward run with real video, either by adding verifiable real-video questions (V+R) or by mixing in unverified data (V+U). In our grid, both remedies held out-of-domain accuracy at base level where verified-only training produced an otherwise undetected 27-point regression, and mixing never degraded performance on any model.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our largest model is 12B parameters and our optimizer budget is 1,200 steps per run; stronger effects may exist at scale. The V+R arm tests a single augmentation source on a single model; a full grid of augmentation sources and models would strengthen the causal claim. The stress set, while built from temporal questions on real video, inherits NExT-QA’s multiple-choice format, and we measure grounding only through order destruction; causal-edge or counterfactual-consistency evaluations [ 16 , 15 ] are complementary. Two candidate model families were excluded for infrastructure incompatibilities rather than scientific reasons.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We conducted a controlled, multi-model study of reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards for causal–temporal video reasoning. The recipe reliably improves in-domain accuracy, but decomposition shows that much of the improvement is non-visual; out-of-domain transfer degrades severely under narrow synthetic-only verified data and is preserved by diversifying the training distribution with real video, whether verified or unverified; and no recipe altered temporal-order grounding, which remained null under a diagnostic specifically designed to detect it. Verifiable rewards are satisfied by whatever capabilities a model can most readily improve; inducing genuine temporal grounding appears to require reward constructions for which temporal integration is the only means of obtaining credit.

A Controlled Multi-Model Study Avyay Sadhu Patrick Cooper Affiliation: University of Colorado Boulder Abstract Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has produced large reasoning gains in language models, and verifiable video benchmarks make the recipe directly applicable to causal–temporal video question answering. We present a controlled study of what RLVR actually teaches video–language models about temporal structure. We fine-tune four open models (Qwen3-VL-8B/4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) under three data recipes: verified (synthetic CLEVRER-derived questions with exact answer and event-order rewards), unverified (self-supervised pretext tasks over 43,751 real web videos), and a 1:1 mixture , plus a targeted verified+real arm that augments the verified data with 4,000 verifiable questions on real video. A pre-registered protocol evaluates every model–recipe cell on a held-out in-domain test set and on out-of-domain real video: a temporal stress set built from NExT-QA and a broad-coverage subset of the MVBench temporal benchmark, each under three input conditions: frames in true order, frames shuffled, and no frames. We report four findings. (1) Verified-reward training yields large in-domain gains that shrink as base competence grows (+14 to +19 points on weaker models; +6 on the strongest base model). (2) A substantial fraction of the gain is non-visual: accuracy with no frames rises nearly as much as accuracy with frames, indicating the policy learns answer priors and format in addition to perception. (3) Verified-only training can severely degrade out-of-domain competence without any indication during training: Qwen3-VL-8B loses 26.7 and 25.2 points on the two independent real-video test sets, with losses distributed across every question category, whereas the mixed recipe never significantly degrades any model trained on it, on either set. The verified+real arm removes the degradation ( − 2.3 -2.3 points, within noise of base) while retaining a + 9.3 +9.3 -point in-domain gain, isolating narrow synthetic-only data, rather than verification itself, as the cause. (4) No recipe induces temporal-order grounding, operationalized as the paired ordered-versus-shuffled accuracy difference: across 41 evaluations this diagnostic is statistically indistinguishable from zero in 39 and marginal in the remaining two, even though training explicitly rewarded event ordering and the stress set targets order-dependent questions. We conclude that verifiable rewards improve benchmark accuracy without conferring temporal understanding, that no-frame controls should accompany reported gains, and that diversifying the training distribution with real video – whether verified or unverified – provides an effective safeguard against out-of-domain degradation. We release the full training, evaluation, and analysis pipeline. Figure 1 : Verifiable-reward training improves benchmark accuracy in part without vision. Error bars are 95% clustered-bootstrap CIs; dotted line is 4-way chance. 1 Introduction Film editors have long exploited the fact that the meaning of a sequence of images depends on their order: the Kuleshov effect and the montage tradition demonstrate that viewers construct causal and narrative interpretations from juxtaposition rather than from shots in isolation [ 9 , 5 , 2 ] . For video–language models this classical observation yields a concrete, falsifiable test: a model that genuinely uses temporal structure should lose accuracy when the frames it conditions on are shuffled, whereas a model that answers from per-frame content alone should not. Prior work, including our own, has found that frame-order sensitivity in current models is weak or absent even on causal benchmarks [ 14 ] . A natural hypothesis is that this deficiency is a training problem. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards has recently produced significant reasoning improvements in language models [ 17 , 4 , 12 ] : when the correctness of an output can be checked programmatically, policy optimization can climb the reward without human preference labels. Causal–temporal video QA appears ideally suited to this recipe. Synthetic benchmarks such as CLEVRER [ 19 ] provide exact answers, ground-truth event orders, and unlimited generation, so a reward can score not only the final answer but the temporal claims a model makes along the way. If any training signal can teach a model to use frame order, a reward that credits correctly ordered events should. This paper asks, with a controlled experimental design, what RLVR training actually changes in a video–language model. Three properties are distinguishable and, we show, empirically separable: (i) in-domain answer accuracy; (ii) transfer of that accuracy to out-of-domain, real-video questions; and (iii) temporal grounding, operationalized as the paired ordered-versus-shuffled accuracy difference on held-out items. Our design crosses four open model families with three data recipes – verified synthetic data with exact rewards, unverified real video with self-supervised pretext rewards, and a 1:1 mixture – plus a targeted fourth arm that augments the verified data with real-video verifiable questions, and evaluates every cell under a pre-registered protocol with clustered bootstrap confidence intervals, disjoint train/test scene splits, and cryptographic test-set fingerprints to guarantee identical items across comparisons. The results separate the three properties cleanly. Verified-reward GRPO reliably improves in-domain accuracy, with gains inversely related to the base model’s initial competence. However, a blind control, in which the model is evaluated with no frames at all, reveals that a large share of the gain is non-visual: policies acquire benchmark priors and answer formatting alongside any perceptual improvement. Out of domain, the verified-only recipe proves hazardous: Qwen3-VL-8B lost 26.7 and 25.2 points on two independent real-video test sets after verified-only training, whereas models trained on the mixture never significantly degraded, and augmenting the verified data with real verified questions restored base-level transfer – isolating data narrowness, not verification, as the cause. Finally, on the property the reward most directly targeted, we observe no effect: across 41 model–recipe–test evaluations, shuffling the input frames produced no reliable loss of accuracy in any condition, including on a stress set of questions selected to require temporal order. To our knowledge, this is the first multi-model, multi-recipe controlled study of verifiable-reward reinforcement learning for video reasoning. It establishes that the accuracy gains such training produces should not be interpreted as temporal understanding, that no-frame controls are necessary to audit what was learned, and that incorporating inexpensive unverified video into the training distribution constitutes an effective safeguard against out-of-domain degradation at negligible additional cost. The ordered/shuffled/blind evaluation protocol, the reward suite with its anti-gaming guards, and the full pipeline are released for reuse. 2 Related Work Temporal order and montage. That ordered juxtaposition creates meaning absent from individual images is foundational in film theory: Kuleshov’s editing experiments [ 9 ] and Eisenstein’s montage writings [ 5 ] document that interpretation is constructed between shots, a view elaborated by modern film scholarship [ 2 ] . We adopt this observation as motivation for a diagnostic – if meaning derives from order, then destroying order should impair a system that genuinely exploits it – rather than as a novel claim. In machine learning, shuffling and single-frame controls have shown that video–language benchmarks are often solvable without temporal information [ 3 , 13 ] ; those studies characterize benchmarks and pretrained models , whereas we ask whether targeted reinforcement learning can change the property, extending the control to paired per-item statistics with clustered uncertainty estimates measured before and after training. Causal–temporal video benchmarks. CLEVRER [ 19 ] isolates collision causality with descriptive, explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual questions over synthetic physics scenes and provides exact ground truth, making it a natural source of verifiable rewards. NExT-QA [ 18 ] targets temporal and causal questions on real web video. MVBench [ 10 ] assembles twenty temporal subtasks from ground-truth annotations of six video sources, VCRBench [ 16 ] evaluates long-form causal chains via clip reordering, and ChainReaction [ 15 ] structures causal-why QA around explicit causal chains. We train on CLEVRER-derived items (verified arm) and evaluate out-of-domain transfer on NExT-QA-derived temporal items and a broad MVBench subset, keeping all test sets video-disjoint from all training data. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. Group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [ 17 ] optimizes a policy against group-normalized rewards without a value network and underlies recent reasoning-focused post-training [ 4 ] . RLVR [ 12 ] formalizes training against programmatically checkable answers. Applications to multimodal models have focused on answer-level rewards for image reasoning; systematic evidence about what such training changes in video models – beyond benchmark scores – is scarce. Our study fills this gap with controls (shuffled and blind inputs, out-of-domain sets) designed to decompose the learned change. Self-supervised video pretext tasks. Temporal pretext tasks – ordering shuffled clips, verifying arrow of time, anticipating future frames – have a long history in video representation learning. Our unverified arm ports these ideas to policy optimization: rewards are computed from the video itself (e.g., reconstructing the true position of frames), so tens of thousands of unlabeled web videos [ 6 ] become training signal with no annotation cost. 3 Method 3.1 Policy optimization Let π θ \pi_{\theta} be a vision–language model that maps a prompt x x (interleaved instruction text and K K video frames) to a text completion y y . For each training prompt we sample a group of G G completions y 1 , … , y G ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y_{1},\dots,y_{G}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) , score each with a scalar reward R ⁡ ( y g , x ) R(y_{g},x) (Sec. 3.2 ), and apply GRPO [ 17 ] : the advantage of y g y_{g} is its reward standardized within the group, A g = R ⁡ ( y g , x ) − mean g ′ ⁡ R ⁡ ( y g ′ , x ) std g ′ ⁡ R ⁡ ( y g ′ , x ) , A_{g}\;=\;\frac{R(y_{g},x)-\operatorname{mean}_{g^{\prime}}R(y_{g^{\prime}},x)}{\operatorname{std}_{g^{\prime}}R(y_{g^{\prime}},x)}, (1) and the policy gradient is taken on token log-probabilities weighted by A g A_{g} . We use G = 8 G{=}8 completions per prompt, LoRA adapters [ 8 ] (rank 32, α = 64 \alpha{=}64 , dropout 0.05, attention projections) on a frozen bf16 base model, learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , effective batch size 8 prompts per step, and 1,200 optimizer steps per run. Sampling uses a colocated vLLM engine [ 11 ] with per-token truncated importance-sampling correction between the sampler and trainer log-probabilities. 1 1 1 The library default, which masks whole sequences on the exponentiated sum of per-token discrepancies, silently zeroes essentially all gradients at realistic vision–language numerics; the supplementary material documents this and other failure modes we corrected, each of which produced healthy-looking but non-learning runs. Each prompt carries K = 8 K{=}8 frames sampled uniformly from the clip, capped at 401,408 401{,}408 pixels per frame. After training, adapters are merged into the base weights and all evaluation is performed on the merged model by the same serving stack used for base models, so trained and untrained checkpoints are measured identically. 3.2 Verifiable rewards The reward is a weighted sum R = r ans + r ord + 0.2 ​ r fmt R=r_{\text{ans}}+r_{\text{ord}}+0.2\,r_{\text{fmt}} of three programmatically checkable terms. Definition 1 (Answer reward) For multiple-choice items with gold letter a ⋆ a^{\star} and choice set C C , r ans ( y ) = 𝟏 [ parse ( y ) = a ⋆ ] r_{\text{ans}}(y)=\mathbf{1}[\operatorname{parse}(y)=a^{\star}] , where parse \operatorname{parse} extracts the letter from a delimited answer block and accepts only members of C C . Definition 2 (Order reward) For items with a ground-truth event or clip order σ ⋆ \sigma^{\star} over n n elements, the completion’s stated order σ ^ \hat{\sigma} is parsed from the answer block; r ord ​ ( y ) = ( τ ⁡ ( σ ^ , σ ⋆ ) + 1 ) / 2 r_{\text{ord}}(y)=(\tau(\hat{\sigma},\sigma^{\star})+1)/2 , where τ \tau is the Kendall rank correlation, and r ord = 0 r_{\text{ord}}{=}0 if no order is parseable. r fmt r_{\text{fmt}} pays small credit for a structured response (a scene summary, a causal chain that cites specific frames, and a delimited answer). Two guards prevent reward gaming, both added after observed exploits: blocks that parrot the instruction text earn nothing, and order parsing is restricted to the delimited answer block so that frame citations inside chain-of-thought text cannot be harvested as an ordering the model never asserted. Reward terms that are constant within a completion group cancel exactly in Eq. 1 ; we verified each term has within-group variance on real batches. 3.3 Three data recipes Verified (V). Multiple-choice and event-ordering items derived from CLEVRER [ 19 ] train scenes, where r ans r_{\text{ans}} and r ord r_{\text{ord}} are exact. Train, validation, and test splits are scene-disjoint. Unverified (U). Self-supervised pretext items over FineVideo [ 6 ] , a corpus of 43,751 43{,}751 real web videos (3,425 hours) we ingest and segment. Tasks include temporal jigsaw (recover the true position of shuffled frames) and anticipation (select which candidate frame follows a prefix). Both are scored by the reward terms of Sec. 3.2 – r ord r_{\text{ord}} over the stated frame order for jigsaw, r ans r_{\text{ans}} over the candidate choice for anticipation – with ground truth computed from the video itself, so no annotation is used and no reward term is unique to either arm. Held-out videos are excluded at the corpus level. Mixed (V+U). A 1:1 interleaving of the two sources at the prompt level, holding total optimization steps fixed, so the comparison against V isolates the effect of diversifying the reward distribution rather than training longer. Verified+Real (V+R). A targeted arm, run on Qwen3-VL-8B, that keeps every reward term and hyperparameter of V but augments the CLEVRER items with 4,000 4{,}000 multiple-choice questions from the NExT-QA train split (causal and temporal types), whose exact answers make them verifiable. Because V and V+R differ only in training data, the comparison separates two candidate causes of any out-of-domain effect of V: verified-reward optimization itself versus the narrowness of a single synthetic source. As this arm trains on NExT-QA, the temporal stress set (built from the video-disjoint validation split, Sec. 4 ) is near-domain rather than out-of-domain for it; the MVBench set remains fully out of domain for every arm. 3.4 Models We train Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B [ 1 ] , and Gemma-3-12B [ 7 ] – two vendors, two architecture generations, and a 3 × \times scale range. All four receive the V recipe; the three Qwen models receive all three recipes, and Qwen3-VL-8B additionally receives the V+R arm (the Gemma U/V+U cells did not complete within our compute budget and are omitted rather than partially reported). Two further candidates were excluded for cause, documented in the supplementary material: Gemma-3-4B scores below the random floor on the task (0.3% ordered accuracy), which makes every GRPO group’s rewards identical and the gradient identically zero; and InternVL3.5-14B / VideoLLaMA3-7B could not be served faithfully by the sampling stack (dynamic-tiling and unsupported-architecture incompatibilities, respectively). 4 Evaluation protocol Test sets. The in-domain set contains n = 300 n{=}300 multiple-choice items from CLEVRER validation scenes, scene-disjoint from all training data. Two out-of-domain sets probe transfer to real video. The temporal stress set contains n = 300 n{=}300 multiple-choice items built from NExT-QA [ 18 ] temporal questions. The broad set contains n = 306 n{=}306 items sampled evenly from nine MVBench [ 10 ] subtasks spanning six source datasets (SSv2, Moments-in-Time, FunQA, Perception Test, MoVQA scenes, and VLN); we exclude MVBench’s five CLEVRER-derived subtasks, whose videos share our verified training domain, along with license-gated, frame-folder-format, and segment-bounded subtasks (scoping rationale in the supplementary material). Every evaluation embeds a SHA-256 fingerprint of its item identifiers in its output; all evaluations of a given test set share one fingerprint, so every reported comparison is over identical items. Input conditions. Each item is evaluated under three conditions: ordered (frames in true temporal order), shuffled (the same frames, deterministically permuted per item), and blind (no frames). Ordered accuracy measures task performance; the paired ordered − - shuffled difference measures temporal grounding; blind accuracy measures how much of the task is solvable from the question text and learned priors alone. Definition 3 (Order sensitivity) For items i = 1 , … , n i=1,\dots,n with per-item correctness c i ord , c i shuf ∈ { 0 , 1 } c^{\mathrm{ord}}_{i},c^{\mathrm{shuf}}_{i}\in\{0,1\} , order sensitivity is Δ ord = 1 n ​ ∑ i ( c i ord − c i shuf ) \Delta_{\mathrm{ord}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i}(c^{\mathrm{ord}}_{i}-c^{\mathrm{shuf}}_{i}) , with uncertainty from a bootstrap that resamples videos (clusters), not items. Statistics. All intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap CIs with cluster resampling at the video level, which is conservative when multiple items share a source video. Decoding is greedy (temperature 0 0 ) for all evaluations. The harness refuses items without a well-formed multiple-choice prompt and reports error, empty-response, and structured-format rates alongside accuracy; no reported evaluation produced an errored or empty generation, so differences are not artifacts of failed generations. We report uncertainty intervals throughout rather than binary significance tests; with 41 evaluation cells, readers should interpret individual marginal intervals with the usual multiplicity caution – our conclusions rest on the direction and consistency of effects across models, not on any single cell. Reproducibility. Every number in this paper is generated by script from archived evaluation artifacts; no result is transcribed by hand. Data builds, splits, and frame shuffling are deterministic (fixed seeds), training uses a pinned configuration per arm with a run-signature guard that refuses to resume a checkpoint under changed semantics, and evaluations embed the test-set fingerprint they were scored on. We organize the results as four findings. 5.1 Verified rewards improve in-domain accuracy inversely to base competence Every model improves in-domain under the V recipe: + 14.3 +14.3 points on Qwen3-VL-8B ( 0.467 → 0.610 0.467\to 0.610 ), + 17.3 +17.3 on Qwen3-VL-4B, + 19.3 +19.3 on Gemma-3-12B, and + 6.3 +6.3 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. The ordering is informative: Qwen2.5-VL-7B begins with the highest accuracy ( 0.607 0.607 ) and gains the least, with all three of its recipes statistically indistinguishable from one another, whereas the two weakest initial models (Gemma-3-12B at 0.083 0.083 , Qwen3-VL-4B at 0.147 0.147 ) gain the most. Verifiable-reward reinforcement learning is thus most effective precisely where the base model has not already internalized the task, and its returns diminish sharply with base competence. The recipes differentiate by model. On Qwen3-VL-8B the unverified recipe reduces in-domain accuracy ( − 7.7 -7.7 ), as pretext tasks alone draw the policy away from the benchmark distribution, whereas on Qwen3-VL-4B the same recipe is the most effective single source ( + 22.0 +22.0 ). The mixture is never the worst recipe and is the best on Qwen3-VL-4B ( + 25.7 +25.7 ). 5.2 A blind control reveals non-visual gains Accuracy with no frames rises under training in nearly every cell: 0.263 → 0.420 0.263\to 0.420 on Qwen3-VL-8B (V), 0.147 → 0.383 0.147\to 0.383 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B (V+U). Because the blind condition contains no visual information, this gain is attributable entirely to prior and format learning: the policy learns which answers are likely and how to express them. The effect transfers out of domain: on the MVBench subset, the blind accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B rises from 0.150 0.150 at base to 0.395 0.395 – 0.431 0.431 under every recipe (Table 3 ); much of what RLVR training imparts survives domain shift precisely because it never depended on the visual input. The visually attributable gain, ordered accuracy minus blind accuracy, changes far less: for Qwen3-VL-8B it is 0.203 0.203 at base and 0.190 0.190 after verified training. A benchmark improvement of 14 points therefore decomposes into predominantly non-visual learning that a standard evaluation would have attributed to perception. We contend that no-frame controls should be standard practice when reporting reinforcement learning gains on multimodal benchmarks. 5.3 Verified-only training degrades out-of-domain competence; mixing is protective Figure 2 : The verified-only collapse replicates on two independent out-of-domain test sets, and diversifying the verified data removes it (colors as in Fig. 1 ). Verified-only training costs Qwen3-VL-8B 26.7 points on the NExT-QA temporal stress set and 25.2 points on the MVBench broad subset; the verified+real arm (light blue), which differs from verified only in its training data, remains at base level on both sets, and the mixed recipe remains statistically indistinguishable from base or improves upon it in every cell. Error bars are 95% clustered-bootstrap CIs. On the real-video stress set (Table 2 , Fig. 2 a), verified-only training severely degraded Qwen3-VL-8B: the model falls from 0.707 0.707 to 0.440 0.440 ordered accuracy, a 26.7 26.7 -point regression on a domain its training never touched, with losses distributed broadly across items (95 items lost against 15 gained) and across all three temporal question categories (per-category breakdown in the supplementary material). The degradation replicates on the MVBench broad subset (Table 3 , Fig. 2 b): the same checkpoint falls from 0.621 0.621 to 0.369 0.369 ( − 25.2 -25.2 ), declining on every one of the nine subtasks, most severely on character ordering ( 0.853 → 0.118 0.853\to 0.118 ), despite training that directly rewarded event ordering. The same recipe does not degrade models with weaker base performance: Qwen3-VL-4B gains out of domain on both sets ( + 2.7 +2.7 stress, + 8.2 +8.2 broad) and Gemma-3-12B gains + 22.2 +22.2 on the broad set. The failure is therefore model-dependent, and, critically, it is undetectable from the training signal: neither the reward curves nor in-domain validation distinguishes the two outcomes. The mixed recipe never significantly degraded any model on either out-of-domain set (largest decline − 3.9 -3.9 points, with confidence intervals overlapping base; up to + 11.4 +11.4 on Qwen3-VL-4B) while retaining roughly two-thirds of the verified in-domain gain on the 8B model and all of it on the 4B model. Unverified real-video data thus serves a regularizing role: its rewards cannot be satisfied through benchmark-specific priors, and it anchors the policy to the distribution on which deployment occurs. Isolating the cause. The collapse admits two explanations: verified-reward optimization itself narrows the policy, or the verified data is too narrow (a single synthetic source). The V+R arm separates them, because it changes only the data: same rewards, same hyperparameters, with 4,000 4{,}000 real-video verifiable questions added to the CLEVRER items. On MVBench, which remains fully out of domain for this arm, the degradation disappears: 0.598 0.598 against a base of 0.621 0.621 ( − 2.3 -2.3 points, confidence intervals overlapping), where V lost 25.2 25.2 . The arm simultaneously retains a + 9.3 +9.3 -point in-domain gain ( 0.467 → 0.560 0.467\to 0.560 , Table 1 ), about two-thirds of V’s, and matches base on the (for this arm, near-domain) stress set ( 0.697 0.697 vs. 0.707 0.707 ). The out-of-domain collapse is therefore a property of narrow synthetic-only verified data rather than of verifiable rewards as such, and it has two effective remedies at equal compute: diversify the verified data with real-video questions (V+R), or mix in unverified real video (V+U). 5.4 No recipe induces temporal-order grounding Figure 3 : Order sensitivity is null essentially everywhere. Thirty-nine intervals cross zero, and the two exceptions are marginal (lower bounds ≤ 0.01 \leq 0.01 ) and inconsistent across recipes and test sets. Across all 41 evaluations (Fig. 3 ) – four models, up to four recipes, three test sets – the order-sensitivity estimate Δ ord \Delta_{\mathrm{ord}} is statistically indistinguishable from zero in 39 cells, with point estimates as often negative as positive; the two interval exceptions (Qwen3-VL-4B base and unverified on the broad set, lower bounds 0.010 0.010 and 0.003 0.003 ) are marginal, do not persist across recipes or test sets, and are consistent with what multiplicity predicts at this cell count. The null holds (i) on the stress set constructed specifically from temporal questions, (ii) after training in which event ordering was directly and substantially rewarded ( r ord r_{\text{ord}} at full weight), and (iii) for every recipe, including the one that improved in-domain accuracy by 25.7 points and the V+R arm trained directly on real-video temporal questions. Models improve on temporal benchmarks while remaining indifferent to temporal order : they answer from per-frame content, question priors, and, on synthetic data, learned answer statistics. We conclude that answer- and order-level verifiable rewards, at this scale and with this optimizer, do not induce temporal grounding; optimization instead exploits capabilities that are more readily improved, and these suffice to saturate the reward. 6 Discussion Why rewards fail to reach temporal structure. Policy optimization preferentially exploits whichever sources of reward are most readily improved. Our decomposition identifies at least three such sources that require less capability change than order grounding: answer-format compliance (immediate reward from r fmt r_{\text{fmt}} and parseability), question/answer priors (visible in the blind gains), and per-frame recognition (sufficient for most benchmark items, as the shuffled condition demonstrates). A reward that assigns credit only when order is decision-relevant – for instance, items constructed so that the shuffled answer differs from the ordered answer – is a natural next step; our results establish that merely rewarding correct orderings of recognizable events is insufficient, because the events can be ordered from appearance cues without temporal integration. Practical guidance. For practitioners applying RLVR to video models, our results support three recommendations: report no-frame controls alongside headline gains; evaluate at least one out-of-domain set before and after training, with identical items enforced by fingerprinting; and diversify the training distribution of any verified-reward run with real video, either by adding verifiable real-video questions (V+R) or by mixing in unverified data (V+U). In our grid, both remedies held out-of-domain accuracy at base level where verified-only training produced an otherwise undetected 27-point regression, and mixing never degraded performance on any model. Limitations. Our largest model is 12B parameters and our optimizer budget is 1,200 steps per run; stronger effects may exist at scale. The V+R arm tests a single augmentation source on a single model; a full grid of augmentation sources and models would strengthen the causal claim. The stress set, while built from temporal questions on real video, inherits NExT-QA’s multiple-choice format, and we measure grounding only through order destruction; causal-edge or counterfactual-consistency evaluations [ 16 , 15 ] are complementary. Two candidate model families were excluded for infrastructure incompatibilities rather than scientific reasons. 7 Conclusion We conducted a controlled, multi-model study of reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards for causal–temporal video reasoning. The recipe reliably improves in-domain accuracy, but decomposition shows that much of the improvement is non-visual; out-of-domain transfer degrades severely under narrow synthetic-only verified data and is preserved by diversifying the training distribution with real video, whether verified or unverified; and no recipe altered temporal-order grounding, which remained null under a diagnostic specifically designed to detect it. Verifiable rewards are satisfied by whatever capabilities a model can most readily improve; inducing genuine temporal grounding appears to require reward constructions for which temporal integration is the only means of obtaining credit.
